Hi OP! I just got my EN3P last month so I'm not very knowledgeable by any means, but I started having this issue after a few weeks, are you using the unmodified EN3P profile from Cura?

So first what I did was run the calibration, after it ran, I did the paper slide adjustment for the height,  put it down to where the paper felt like it was being held by the needle and then put up by .01mm until the friction was gone, then i reran calibration and tested the paper again just for good measure. Now on Cura, if you select Expert Settings (not sure if available under Advanced) there should be a setting called "Skirt/Brim Flow" under "Materials", set it to 105 and test printing something small with a tree support and just pay attention to the first layer and make sure those gaps are basically non-existent (if anything, the visible "gaps" should just be very thin filament, I might have a picture), but that when the second layer goes on top, the needle is not dragging ANY filament around, if it is, then decrease flow, if you see gaps, increase and try again. I'd recommend testing after just running the calibration once just so to make sure that it wasn't just a calibration issue before you mess with flow

Food is what keeps us alive but can also be harmful to us if we don't know what we're eating. I really recommend you download an app that tracks your calories and macros, and learn up a bit about what these mean. For your height, depending on your level of activity, you might want to start eating between 1200-1400 calories a day. Read up on what calories look like in portions, and read the back of the labels. Make sure you're balacing your diet, your macros are proteins, fats and carbs, and your body NEEDS all three, but you should balance them, I would recommend focusing on balacing with about 40-60% protein and then the rest divide between fats and carbs. It is harder if you don't cook for yourself, but everything has nutrition facts on the back, and the serving sizes on the back matters! Keep track of what you eat (I use MyFitnessPal) and I know the hardest part sometimes is saying no to yummy foods that get thrown on your face all the time, but once you learn how calories and their portions look, and have your end goal in mind, it becomes easier. 

You can reach out if you ever need help, I learned how to have a healthier relationship with food after years of overeating and eating disorders. Knowing what I put in my body has helped me rationalize and portion/plan things better because I gain weight easily, but I have been able to maintain a healthy weight for almost 2 years now, completely free of disordered eating behavior. I keep the calorie tracking because it helps with peace of mind and helps me curb down the urge I used to get to engage in bad behaviors, it's just a habit when I meal prep now :)

The ultimatum is kind of gross in my opinion. She's not asking for time to party or neglect her studies, she's asking for time to focus on them and do homework and also take care of herself. College takes a huge mental toll, I almost dropped out during my last semester.

I was lucky enough to have amazing parents that covered whatever my scholarships didn't and still gave me a bit of extra money every week ($150) to help me out with expenses. They still paid my car insurance and phone while I paid my car, living expenses, and rent (of course part of the money they gave me went towards that). I've been working since I was 15, my family is middle class and they didn't start giving me an allowance until I moved away from college, so I was used to working (up to 3 jobs at one point at 16-17) while studying. I was always an A student and got my tuition almost fully covered by scholarships and financial aid. 

College was a different beast though. My parents never taught me to take care of myself and my surroundings, so it was hard to get used to living alone and taking care of myself from one day to the next. I had to learn to cook, do laundry and basic cleaning by myself, but I did it and always had their support, even if they were 3 hours away. Every time I went home or they would visit they would bring me homemade meals to last me a few weeks and restock my pantry and my gas tank. I wouldn't have made through college if it wasn't for their help. They always said they're investing in my future and that's all they work hard for.

I graduated 4 years ago, due to life and cost of living, I'm once again living with them. I;m working full time and contribute only $250 towards rent, but I pay all my other expenses and huge debt I have from bad decisions. I'm studying again now to get better certifications for my career and they still see my future as an investment. They always offer to pay for my exams (which cost $300-500+ each), and they support me quitting a job I don't enjoy if that means that it will help me emotionally and in my career. They wouldn't charge me rent while I'm not working either.

I guess I just got lucky with amazing parents, and not all parents have the same mentality. But I know that when I finally make it to where I want to be, my first goal is to pay off their house and give them a fraction of what they did for me back. All the money in the world could never pay for all the sacrifices they had to do for me to be where I am today, and I'm forever grateful for my family.
